title: Anatomy of a phishing email
body_md:
## The envelope is not the letter

A phishing email is a request in borrowed clothes. It may ask you to sign in, open a file, pay an invoice, ring a number or hand over a few small details, and it will ask in the voice of someone you already trust. The logo can be flawless and the grammar better than your own. So set the costume aside and put one question to the message: **what does it want me to do, and how can I check that somewhere the message cannot reach?**

### Five things to read, in order

1. **The claim.** The display name, the logo, the tidy footer: they tell you who the sender would like to be, and every one of them can be copied in a minute. Open the sender details and read the real address, but hold the result loosely. A familiar address proves little, because genuine mailboxes get hijacked too.
2. **The nudge.** A deadline, a warning about your account, a prize you never entered for: each is built to hurry you. Honest organisations send urgent notices as well, so urgency alone convicts no one. Pause because the action matters, not because a clock is ticking.
3. **The ask.** Find every link, attachment, reply address and phone number the message wants you to use. A letter with no link can still steer you to a fraudulent helpline. And a password or a one-time code never belongs in a reply.
4. **The destination.** On a computer, hover over a button without clicking; most mail programs will show where it leads. What a button says and where it goes are two separate facts. If the address is shortened, clipped or simply murky, do not settle the matter by following it. A preview shows only the first hop, so once a page has opened, read its address again before you trust it.
5. **The other road.** Open the service’s app or a bookmark you already use, or phone it on a number you found yourself. If the trouble is real, it will usually be waiting for you there. For a request from work, use the channel your workplace already trusts.

No single clue settles it. The sender-check badges some mail programs display are useful, but they do not prove a request is legitimate, and an honest newsletter may arrive through a mailing platform whose domain looks nothing like the brand’s. What decides the matter is the action being asked of you, and whether a second, independent road exists to check it.

### A habit of one breath

Say the claim aloud: “This message says my account needs attention.” Then put the message down, take your usual road, and compare what you find. If you cannot check right now, you can wait. An unexpected email is not owed an instant answer.

widget_config.goal: When an unexpected email arrives, name what it asks you to do and check that claim through a channel you already trust.
widget_config.today_action: Pick one recent service notification in your inbox and leave its links alone. Find the sender details, and decide where you would go to check its claim yourself.
widget_config.scope: Everyday advice for ordinary users. The firms, people and addresses in the examples are invented. Reporting routes and account procedures differ by service and country.

blocks.title: The storage warning
blocks.situation: A polished email from “Cloud Desk” says your storage will be shut down tonight. The sender is help@cloud-desk-alerts.example, the button says “Keep files,” and the page behind it wants your sign-in and a one-time code.
blocks.analysis: A threat of loss plus a request for a code makes the action high-risk before you have read another word. The name and the layout authenticate nothing. Leave the button alone, open your usual storage app or bookmarked site to look at the account itself, and report the message if nothing there confirms it.

blocks.title: A real change of platform
blocks.situation: You booked a train yesterday. Now an email from a ticketing service you recognise says your departure platform has changed. It carries a “View ticket” button and your booking reference.
blocks.analysis: The timing and the reference both fit a genuine notice, but both can be copied, so neither is proof. Open the ticket in the app you bought it from, or check the operator’s official service page. If the change shows up there, you can act on it without ever trusting the link in the email.

blocks.title: The invoice nobody expected
blocks.setup: An invented exercise: an email arrives with an invoice for a software subscription. No real message or account is involved.

steps.prompt: The display name matches the service, but you were not expecting a bill. What do you do first?

choices.text: Work out what the email is asking, and leave the attachment closed.
choices.consequence: You have kept the evidence and exposed nothing.
choices.explanation: Start from the request, not from the wrapper.

choices.text: Open the attachment to see whether it is genuine.
choices.consequence: The file opens before you know where it came from.
choices.explanation: An unexpected file may be the attack itself. Examine the claim before you touch it.

steps.prompt: The message says your payment failed and offers a support number. How do you check?

choices.text: Call the number printed in the email.
choices.consequence: Your call may be answered by whoever wrote the message.
choices.explanation: A copied footer can carry a number the attacker controls.

choices.text: Open your subscription app or a bookmarked account page.
choices.consequence: You can look at your billing by a route you set up yourself.
choices.explanation: Arriving by your own road tests the claim without using the path it offered you.

steps.prompt: Later you check the real account through your bookmark. There is no unpaid invoice. What now?

choices.text: Report the suspicious email through your mail program or your workplace’s process.
choices.consequence: The message goes to the people who review such things.
choices.explanation: Report the mismatch, but do not count on a report to block every copy at once.

choices.text: Reply and ask the sender to explain.
choices.consequence: You walk back into a conversation you cannot trust.
choices.explanation: A reply establishes nothing about who is writing, and it may invite more pressure.

steps.prompt: A colleague says the same email reached them. How do you help?

choices.text: Forward the live email so they can take a look.
choices.consequence: A working link or attachment lands in one more inbox.
choices.explanation: Use your organisation’s reporting channel instead of passing along something that still works.

choices.text: Tell them the claim did not check out, and point them to the proper way to report it.
choices.consequence: They can check their own account and report their own copy.
choices.explanation: It gives them a safe next step without spreading the message.

blocks.debrief: Neither the polish nor the familiar name settled anything about the invoice; the real account did. Go back and retry any decision to find the moment where the email tried to steer you.

questions.prompt: A message from a familiar address asks for a one-time sign-in code. What is safest?

choices.text: Send it, because the address is familiar.
choices.explanation: The address or the account may be in someone else’s hands, and a code can unlock an account.

choices.text: Do not send it; check the request through your usual channel.
choices.explanation: The action is unsafe however familiar the wrapper looks.

questions.prompt: A well-written alert says you must update your payment details tonight. What does the good grammar prove?

choices.explanation: Polished text is easy to produce.

choices.text: Nothing about who has the right to ask. Check your billing in the app or site you already use.
choices.explanation: The claim still needs independent checking.

questions.prompt: A genuine-looking ticket update arrives soon after your purchase. What do you do?

choices.text: Look at your ticket in the app or the operator’s site that you already use.
choices.explanation: A plausible message can still be checked without its link.

choices.text: Assume it is fake, since real notices never contain buttons.
choices.explanation: Real notices often have buttons. The button just isn’t your means of checking.

questions.prompt: A suspicious email has no link, only a support number to call. Is that safe?

choices.explanation: A phone number can be exactly where the attacker wants you to land.

choices.text: Not necessarily; find the service’s number yourself.
choices.explanation: A request to call needs the same independent check as a request to click.
